prompt: Three teams built the checkout flow, and it ended up as exactly three services with awkward hand-offs where the teams meet.
trap: It wasn't a technical decision; the org chart made it.

prompt: Leadership wants one unified platform but keeps four separate teams that rarely talk. Architects predict four platforms.
tells: four separate teams that rarely talk
why: To get the architecture you want, shape the teams to match it (the "inverse Conway maneuver").
trap: A diagram alone won't override how people communicate.

prompt: The public API has separate endpoints for "billing customers" and "support customers" because two departments own customer data.
why: The org split leaked into the product's interface.
trap: Users don't care about your departments; the API shows them anyway.

prompt: Bugs keep piling up in the shared library that sits between two teams, because neither team considers it theirs.
why: Components without a clear owning team rot; ownership boundaries shape system quality.
trap: Better code review won't fix a missing owner.

prompt: A company with 12 small teams ended up with almost exactly 12 microservices, even where one service would have been simpler.
trap: Count matching that closely is the giveaway.

prompt: To get a clean separation between search and recommendations, the CTO first split one team into two, each owning one side.
tells: first split one team into two
why: The inverse Conway maneuver: shape teams to match the architecture you want.
trap: It's a deliberate use of the law, not a reorg for its own sake.

prompt: The code written by the Berlin team and the code by the Austin team talk only through a narrow message queue, even though both run in one process.
why: Teams that can't talk often build a narrow interface between their parts; distance in the org becomes a seam in the code.
trap: The queue isn't there for latency or partitions; it's there because the teams rarely talk.

prompt: A bank's iOS, Android and web apps each handle login differently, matching the three separate teams that built them.
why: Without a shared owner, each team's design reflects its own structure.
trap: Inconsistency is a symptom; the cause is the org chart.
